item.title: Rocket Report: Artemis II literally tore through the atmosphere; New Glenn delay - Ars Technica
item.description:
Welcome to Edition 9.18 of the Rocket Report! Blue Origin packed a lot of news into one afternoon Thursday with the reveal of a new kick stage for the New Glenn rocket, a new rocket engine design, and the minor and widely expected delay for New Glenn’s return-to-flight mission from December until January. The reconstruction of Blue Origin’s wrecked launch pad at Cape Canaveral, Florida, continues apace after a catastrophic explosion nearly six months ago. There’s a lot of pent-up demand from NASA, Amazon, and the Space Force for Blue Origin to get New Glenn back in action.

As always, we welcome reader submissions, and if you don’t want to miss an issue, please subscribe using the box below (the form will not appear on AMP-enabled versions of the site). Each report will include information on small-, medium-, and heavy-lift rockets as well as a quick look ahead at the next three launches on the calendar.

SpaceX vets work on water-fed propulsion. Three brothers who worked at SpaceX in the Falcon 9 era are now building satellites that run on water, a potentially harvestable resource on the Moon and found all over the Solar System, Ars reports. In late 2022, the three Carlisle brothers founded Argo Space to build infrastructure in space. Their vision was not just in-space transportation but also removing the need to use propellants from Earth to move around the heavens. Argo Space’s satellites will use water not only as a propellant, but also as a coolant and radiation shield.

How does this work? … Argo Space flew its first mission in July, but the spacecraft failed after one of its solar arrays didn’t deploy, and there wasn’t enough time to test the propulsion system. Two more missions are on Argo Space’s schedule for 2027 to demonstrate the company’s water-based thrusters. The propulsion system is basically a small rocket that uses hydrogen and oxygen as propellants. However, instead of launching with separate tanks of liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen, the satellite carries a reservoir of liquid water. In space, the vehicle uses solar power to split water into hydrogen and oxygen gases and burns them to generate thrust.

item.title: Artemis II launch tore a hole in Earth's atmosphere, say scientists - BBC Sky at Night Magazine
item.description:
NASA's Artemis II mission caused enormous disturbances in Earth's atmosphere that scientists say could have disrupted GPS and other communications.

The pre-print study by scientists from National Cheng Kung University in Taiwan found that disturbances created by the launch of the Artemis II rocket were stronger than those caused by any other rocket launches to date.

The team say the research could point to future problems caused by increasingly powerful rocket launches becoming more frequent.

Read more

Read more

A mission around the Moon

The Artemis II mission was arguably the biggest spaceflight story of 2026.

It launched on April 1, 2026, taking four astronauts on a 9-day journey around the Moon and back.

Artemis II travelled further beyond the Moon than any mission before it, using the Moon's gravitational pull to slingshot around it and begin the journey back to Earth.

It was the first crewed mission to the Moon since the Apollo programme and marked a key stepping stone in NASA's plans to establish a permanent human presence on the lunar surface.

A disturbance in Earth's atmosphere

Yet despite the success of the Artemis II mission and its popularity, a pre-print study published in Geophysical Research Letters says that the launch of the Artemis II rocket and subsequent rocket burns caused three distinct disturbances in Earth's ionosphere.

The ionosphere is the region of our atmosphere that reaches about 80–640 km (50–400 miles) above Earth's surface.

It's at the edge of space, marking the boundary between Earth's lower atmosphere and the vacuum of the cosmos.

The first 'disturbance' caused by the Artemis II mission occurred during the rocket's launch from Kennedy Space Center, generating shock-acoustic and gravity wave modulations.

But the next two upper-stage burns were much stronger than the initial liftoff.

An hour after launch, a second disturbance came via the 'apogee raise burn', which is an engine burn used to increase the Artemis II spacecraft's altitude.

About 25 hours after lift-off, a third was caused by the 'trans-lunar injection burn', which is used to put the spacecraft on its journey towards the Moon.

That apogee raise burn "triggered shock waves and unprecedented large-scale disturbances that elongated 50° longitude across North America," the study authors say.

"This is the first time a single space mission produced three instances of ionospheric disturbances over the same region during successive orbit manoeuvres."

Rocket launches, GPS and self-driving cars

One of the key points made by the authors of this pre-print study is the effect that future rocket launches could have on technologies like GPS systems, drones and self-driving cars.

While they found that there was no widespread GPS disruption caused by the Artemis II lift-off itself, they did record changes in the ionosphere that could potentially cause problems during future rocket launches.

Such disturbances could disrupt communications on Earth by, for example, disturbing radio signals.

And rocket launches could affect other technologies on Earth that rely on GPS for positioning, such as self-driving cars and drones.

Read the full study at essopenarchive.org

item.title: You don't have to go to the moon to see Earth differently: Artemis II astronaut Victor Glover on what really matters - Space
item.description:
TENERIFE, Canary Islands — Imagine traveling over 250 million miles from home, watching Earth disappear behind the moon and losing contact with the billions of people who call it home. What would you miss most? For Artemis II astronaut Victor Glover, the answer wasn't a particular place, a familiar view or even the comforts of home. It was something much more fundamental: human connection.

Speaking during a discussion with former astronaut Chris Hadfield at the Starmus VIII festival on Oct. 18 in Tenerife, Canary Islands, Glover reflected on the extraordinary experience of traveling around the moon and how being so far from Earth had given him a renewed appreciation for the people living on it.

"The greatest reason to go to space, it isn't to be a swashbuckler hero," Glover said. "It's to do something that only 651 people have been able to do: miss Earth and miss other Earthlings."

Glover was one of the four astronauts aboard NASA's Artemis II mission, which launched on April 1, 2026, marking humanity's first crewed journey to the moon since Apollo 17 in 1972. Alongside NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman and Christina Koch and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen, the crew traveled farther from Earth than any humans before them.

As the Orion spacecraft traversed the far side of the moon, the Artemis II crew watched Earth disappear below the lunar horizon before losing radio contact with our planet. Around 40 minutes later, Earth came back into view as the spacecraft emerged from behind the moon.

For Glover, however, the experience was about much more than the view. He believes that if everyone on Earth had the opportunity to make the same journey, they would come away with a similar appreciation for what they'd left behind.

"I think all of us would say something in our native language, in the most basic way we can communicate about love, joy, hope and inspiration," Glover said.

Although Glover shared the extraordinary journey with three fellow astronauts, the four of them were separated from the rest of humanity by hundreds of thousands of miles.

And for Glover, that distance brought with it a strange contradiction: the farther he traveled from humanity, the more he longed to connect with it."At the point of ultimate disconnection, [there is] this longing for connection," Glover said.

The experience gave him a perspective that he carried back into everyday life.

"There are moments where I am rushing through traffic and want to get where I'm going because I'm being selfish," Glover admitted. "But I don't have to stay there."

Instead, he remembers what it felt like to look back at a planet so distant that everyone who has ever lived could be covered by his hand.

"I wish you could all feel what it's like to come back home after that disconnection," he said.

The 'sea level effect'

Astronauts often describe experiencing the "overview effect", a profound shift in perspective that can come from seeing Earth from space. But Glover believes that there's something equally powerful waiting to be discovered much closer to home.

When asked by a Starmus VIII attendee whether people needed to undergo something extraordinary to develop a greater sense of kindness toward others, his answer was no.

Glover encouraged people to look more closely at the natural world around them, whether that meant walking along the beach, watching the ocean or simply examining a leaf held up to sunlight. Even something as ordinary as a leaf, he explained, is capable of turning sunlight into food through photosynthesis. And although science can explain how that happens, understanding the process doesn't make it any less remarkable.

"We have to choose to be moved by these things," Glover said.

He worries that modern life, with its endless technological distractions, has made it all too easy to overlook the extraordinary things happening around us.

"Familiarity breeds contempt. Have you heard this? I think it's worse than that. Familiarity breeds indifference," he said.

Glover has a name for this perspective he hopes people can rediscover without traveling into space: The sea level effect.

It's about finding the same sense of wonder and connection that astronauts experience in orbit, but right here on Earth, where most of us spend our lives. And ultimately, Glover believes the greatest wonder isn't the moon, the stars, or even the incredible complexity of nature. It's the people we share our planet with.

"I think the hardest place to see this miracle is in the actual greatest miracle in the universe: other humans," he said.

"We all feel it with babies, but when we get old enough to have opinions, we start to want to argue with each other."

Glover hopes that by taking the time to appreciate the natural world, people might become a little more willing to appreciate one another too.

"That's the mission that I want to be part of for the rest of my life," Glover said.

Daisy Dobrijevic joined Space.com in February 2022, having previously worked as a staff writer for All About Space magazine. She completed an editorial internship with BBC Sky at Night Magazine and worked at the National Space Centre, communicating space science to the public.

Daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.

She will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.

item.title: Meet NASA’s Artemis II Crew During Houston Public Event - NASA (.gov)
item.description:
Editor’s Note: This advisory was updated on Sept. 28, 2026, with ticketing information for the public.

The four astronauts of NASA’s Artemis II mission will participate in an event hosted by industry and community partners at the University of Houston to discuss their mission around the Moon aboard the Orion spacecraft. It will be the first event in Houston for the public following their lunar mission earlier this year and marks the conclusion of their post-flight campaign.

Astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, and Christina Koch of NASA and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Jeremy Hansen will share highlights from their mission at 7 p.m. CDT Wednesday, Sept. 30, during the free, public event at University of Houston’s Fertitta Center. Additionally, the National Aeronautic Association will recognize the crew for surpassing the record for human spaceflight’s farthest distance traveled, previously set by the Apollo 13 mission in 1970.

Media are invited to attend a brief question and answer session with the Artemis II crew at 5:45 p.m. prior to the public presentation. Media interested in attending must RSVP no later than 12 p.m. on Sept. 30 to Kenna Pell at: kenna.m.pell@nasa.gov.

A limited number of tickets to attend the event at no charge are available to the public online. Media are not required to secure a ticket before RSVPing to the event.

NASA’s historic Artemis II mission launched April 1 and splashed down in the Pacific Ocean on April 10. The crew members were the first astronauts to launch on the agency’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket, flying aboard NASA’s Orion spacecraft. During their record-setting mission, the astronauts traveled 252,756 miles from Earth, farther than any humans have traveled before.

As part of the Golden Age of innovation and exploration, NASA will send Artemis astronauts on increasingly difficult missions to explore more of the Moon for scientific discovery, economic benefits, establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface, and to build on our foundation for the first crewed missions to Mars.

item.title: 'Cabin leak suspected': Artemis II astronaut reveals how a warning nearly derailed NASA's epic moon mission - Space
item.description:
TENERIFE, CANARY ISLANDS — NASA's Artemis II astronauts were just minutes away from a critical engine burn that would send them toward the moon when an unexpected cabin leak warning threatened to change the course of their historic mission.

"If it had happened five minutes later, we may not have been able to have that burn," Artemis II pilot Victor Glover revealed during an Oct. 18 discussion with Canadian former astronaut Chris Hadfield at the Starmus VIII festival here in Tenerife.

The incident unfolded on April 2, the second day of the Artemis II mission, as the astronauts' Orion spacecraft swooped back toward Earth after traveling some 38,000 miles (61,000 kilometers) away. Orion had been completing a highly elliptical orbit around Earth, giving the crew and mission control an opportunity to test the capsule's systems before committing to the journey to the moon. Orion was now approaching its closest point to our planet, roughly 100 miles (160 km) above the surface, ahead of the crucial translunar injection (TLI) burn that would send the astronauts moonward.

"Jeremy looks out the window and says, 'I think we're going to run smack dab into the middle of Earth,'" Glover recalled, referring to Artemis II mission specialist Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency. "Because we were getting so low."

The close approach brought additional challenges, as Orion passed through a region populated by orbital debris and satellites.

"The density of things is going up from where we are, and also an increase in radiation," Glover explained.

It was at this particularly demanding point in the mission that Orion issued a warning that indicated a possible cabin leak, around 15 minutes before the critical TLI burn.

"So, determining whether it was real or not was a big deal," Glover said.

The crew and mission control faced a crucial question: Was it safe to continue heading to the moon, or would they have to abandon the planned maneuver and cut the mission very short? "Are we going to do a TLI and burn to go to the moon, or are we putting on our spacesuits to prepare to come back to Earth right now?" Glover recalled.

The timing was particularly critical. The TLI burn was designed to propel Orion out of Earth orbit and onto its trajectory around the moon, marking the first time astronauts had headed toward Earth's nearest neighbor since the Apollo era.

Luckily, as NASA flight director Judd Frieling told us during an April 2 media briefing, the warning turned out to be a false alarm.

So Artemis II received the go-ahead. Orion fired its main engine for approximately five minutes and 50 seconds, successfully setting the four astronauts on their journey around the moon.

"We're watching the timer count down, velocities go up, and the magenta and green numbers coming together," Glover recalled.

"Everything is tracking. It's looking good."

Before long, the crew had broken free of Earth's gravitational hold and were hurtling toward the moon at around 24,500 mph (39,430 kph).

Despite the tense moments before the burn, Artemis II went on to make history. NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman (the mission's commander), Glover (pilot) and Christina Koch (mission specialist), along with Hansen, traveled farther from Earth than any humans before them, reaching a maximum distance of 252,756 miles (406,771 km) during their journey around the moon.

The four astronauts returned safely to Earth on April 10, splashing down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of San Diego after nearly 10 days in space.

item.title: ‘Strong impact:’ Artemis II launch ripped giant holes in Earth’s atmosphere — so much it’s disrupted GPS signals - New York Post
item.description:
The Artemis II astronauts might’ve emerged unscathed from their historic moon mission, but Earth’s navigation equipment might not have been so lucky.

The spacecraft’s April 2026 launch had an unprecedented impact on our planet’s atmosphere, temporarily disrupting GPS systems and potentially causing an accident, according to an alarming study in Geophysical Research Letters.

“It could have a strong impact not only on self-driving cars but also on drone positioning,” study co-author Charles Lin, who teaches earth science at National Cheng Kung University, told Space.com.

NASA’s Artemis II Space Launch System rocket lifts off from Kennedy Space Center on Wednesday, April 1, 2026, in Cape Canaveral, Florida. Getty Images

The study comes seven months after the Artemis II spacecraft safely ferried astronauts to our lunar satellite for the first time in 50 years, hopefully blazing a trail for future moon missions and potentially even colonization.

Following the successful voyage, the researchers observed two giant holes in the ionosphere — the electrically charged region of Earth’s upper atmosphere. These gaps cut 3,100-mile-wide swathes across the American continent, per the study.

The atmospheric perforations formed as Artemis II’s massive core stage blasted through the atmosphere, followed by two engine burns from its upper stage 115 miles above Earth, over an hour after liftoff.

As the thrusters fired, they spewed exhaust that reacted with the ionosphere’s electrically charged particles, creating the resultant disruption like a smaller, more short-lived solar storm.

The researchers determined Artemis II’s ionospheric impact by using data from terrestrial GPS receivers — typically used to measure minute tectonic shifts — to measure how long GPS signals take to travel from the satellites to the Earth receivers.

The solid rocket boosters of NASA’s SLS rocket ignite during the launch of the Artemis II mission. NASA

They found that disturbances in the ionosphere can greatly alter these times.

In fact, the impact generated by the liftoff was more powerful than any other rocket launches observed to date.

And while the shifts in the forcefield’s electron density only translated to positioning errors of several feet, these were more than enough to derail self-driving cars (which have already had their share of snafus), per the study.

“A positioning error of a couple of meters is enough to cause an autonomous car to change lanes,” said Lin.

When extrapolated out, this could wreak havoc on drone navigation as well.

Lin attributed the unusually powerful disturbance to the rocket’s upper stage engines firing directly within the ionosphere — a maneuver that could become increasingly common as humanity ventures further into space.

“Rocket launches from the ground to space produce that kind of effect, but we have never seen this kind of orbital maneuver in an interplanetary mission,” said Lin. “In the future, as we are going to see many more missions going to the Moon and to Mars, these space weather effects will become much more significant.”

item.title: Rigorous Analysis Confirms NASA’s Artemis II Heat Shield Performance - NASA (.gov)
item.description:
NASA’s Artemis II mission sent four astronauts around the Moon and brought them safely back to Earth, laying a foundation for crewed flights to the Moon’s surface.

Additional engineering data analysis of the Orion spacecraft’s heat shield confirmed initial data showing the heat shield performed as expected.

In particular, NASA measured whether the thermal protection system effectively safeguarded the crew and Orion systems as the spacecraft reentered Earth’s atmosphere. This test flight was the first time astronauts flew aboard Orion.

Orion reached a maximum velocity of 39 times the speed of sound and experienced external temperatures exceeding 4,000 degrees Fahrenheit at its peak, all while the four astronauts inside Orion stayed relatively cool with a cabin temperature in the mid-70 degree Fahrenheit range during their return to Earth from the Moon.

After NASA’s thorough analysis of Artemis I heat shield findings, informed by extensive arc jet material testing at NASA’s Ames Research Center in California’s Silicon Valley, the agency modified Orion’s reentry trajectory for Artemis II by shortening the maximum downrange distance the spacecraft could fly between when it entered Earth’s atmosphere and splashed down in the Pacific Ocean. Analysis prior to the mission showed that limiting downrange distance would limit how long the spacecraft’s heat shield spent in the temperature range at which the Artemis I heat shield phenomenon occurred.

The spacecraft reentered with precision, entering within only 192 feet of its targeted entry interface, and successfully splashed down only 0.59 miles from the predicted landing site off the coast of San Diego. Initial inspections of the thermal protection system, including diver imagery of the spacecraft’s heat shield taken just after splashdown and further inspections on the recovery ship, found it performed as expected, with a significant reduction in the amount of cracks and char loss as compared to Artemis I.

Upon the spacecraft’s return to NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida after the Moon mission, thermal protection system experts began additional examination of the heat shield, made of 186 unique blocks of an ablative material called Avcoat. The heat shield was then transported to NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, where work on sample extraction and internal x-ray scans began in August to provide further engineering insight into the system and behavior of the material.

A thorough post-flight assessment review found that Orion’s aerodynamic and aerothermal performance, including the heat shield and backshell thermal protection system, was in line with engineering predictions based on pre-flight analyses and ground testing. The shorter allowable down range during entry reduced the cracking and char loss experienced on the Artemis II heat shield relative to the Artemis I heat shield by a factor of ten, proving the effectiveness of the trajectory modification. Engineers found only nine spots of char loss of varying sizes on the Artemis II heat shield dish, compared to 103 during Artemis I.

The analysis also showed that Orion’s robust heat shield design showed consistency from Artemis I to Artemis II, evident by the performance of system features such as the seams between the heat shield Avcoat blocks and the Avcoat surrounding the heat shield compression pad separation bolts.

Post-flight inspection of Orion’s backshell, the protective cover on the sloped sides of the crew module made up of 1,300 ceramic tiles, showed expected performance across the crew module surface. Visual inspections indicated backshell features designed to seal and protect penetrations such as windows, vents, thrusters, and the side hatch also met expectations, with no signs of overheating observed.

The team also performed post-flight laser scans of the heat shield surface and is comparing this data to pre-flight measurements to determine material recession, which will then be compared to analysis predictions. Engineers are continuing with heat shield sample extraction at NASA Marshall and subsequent material test and assessment and thermal analysis, to support long-term heat shield development, manufacturing efforts, and data capture.

Orion’s performance and the team’s analysis on Artemis II reflect system robustness, capability to support crew, and critical insights gathered that will enhance the Artemis III mission and beyond. Following the extensive Artemis I heat shield investigation, upgrades were made to the heat shield design for Artemis III to achieve uniformity and consistent permeability of the Avcoat blocks. Technicians attached the heat shield for the Artemis III Orion crew module at NASA Kennedy in early July, and the Orion crew and service modules were joined at the end of July. The spacecraft has since been successfully powered up for the first time, enabling engineers to check all connection lines between the two modules are working as planned.

NASA continues to advance toward Artemis III as teams ready the Orion spacecraft for next year’s mission in low Earth orbit. NASA will launch the SLS (Space Launch System) rocket and Orion spacecraft with NASA astronauts Randy Bresnik, Frank Rubio, Andre Douglas, and ESA (European Space Agency) Luca Parmitano, to rendezvous with human lander test articles from Blue Origin and SpaceX to demonstrate critical systems and operations needed for future lunar landings, beginning with Artemis IV in 2028.

item.title: After the applause What Artemis II really means - Room The Space Journal of Asgardia
item.description:
The Artemis II crew returned from a well-publicised lunar flyby mission in mid-April 2026, following a nine-day, one-hour mission. Four astronauts were launched successfully on a free-return trajectory around the Moon and returned safely to a ‘perfect’ splashdown in the Pacific off San Diego. That was good news for the astronauts, for NASA and for the space community in general, but how much did this mission advance the cause of space exploration? Space technologist and author Mark Williamson considers the technology of the recent mission and critiques its presentation by the media. After the emotion of Artemis II comes a more difficult question: what does the mission really mean for the future of human exploration?

Given that no-one has travelled beyond low Earth orbit since December 1972, the Artemis II mission deserves a place in the history books. I grew up in the Apollo era and, it turns out, was sufficiently entranced by the radio and TV coverage to develop a career in the space sector. Since those halcyon days, I have often complained about a lack of action in the space exploration arena, so I should be happy about the Artemis programme… but I can’t quite bring myself to declare a state of nirvana.

Technology

From a purely engineering point of view, the Artemis II mission helped to prove the technology of the Space Launch System (SLS), the Orion capsule and the European Service Module, which is encouraging for future missions.

However, as many commentators have pointed out, Artemis II was effectively a repeat of the Apollo 8 mission of December 1968, which sent three astronauts around the Moon (and, incidentally, produced the famous Earthrise photographs). While it makes sense to test systems this way before committing to a lunar landing, the recent mission was essentially a case of relearning techniques that NASA mastered almost six decades ago – so forgive me if I’m not too excited. The truth of the matter is that this mission was necessary because NASA has lost its ‘institutional memory’ of how to do lunar missions, having been stuck in low Earth orbit for more than half a century!

After the emotion of Artemis II comes a more difficult question: what does the mission really mean for the future of human exploration?

Am I impressed with this 21st century technology, as compared with the launch vehicles and spacecraft launched only 10 years after the first Sputnik? Not really. SLS is styled as NASA’s ‘most powerful rocket’, since its first stage engines produce about 15 percent more thrust than the venerable Saturn V, but the payload capability of the Block I variant to TLI (trans-lunar injection) is only about 60 percent that of the Saturn. In practice, this means that a separate vehicle will be required to place a lander in lunar orbit for the landing mission. On top of this, the development of SLS has been prone to greater delays than the Saturn V; again, I suspect a loss of institutional memory, though lack of sufficient funding has an obvious role to play.

What about the Orion capsule? Well, the word ‘capsule’ is the important one here. Having flown a reusable Space Shuttle orbiter for 30 years, NASA returned to the concept of a capsule with an ablative heatshield similar to that of Apollo (which makes the heatshield issues experienced on Artemis I much less forgivable). True, Orion is half as big again as Apollo in terms of volume, but it’s designed to carry an extra astronaut and enable longer missions so the difference is less significant. It is also intended to be reusable, but this capability has yet to be proven. And, yes, it has a toilet, which replaces the need to defecate in a bag, but was it flawless? No.

Anyone who has ever followed a human space mission knows that the media’s focus on the Orion toilet was a given, whether or not it performed to specification, so why was it allowed to become the focus of media jokes? Why did its design allow even the possibility of a frozen urine vent? It reminded me of an issue with the thrusters on Boeing’s Starliner capsule in 2024, which caused a delay in returning a space station crew to Earth. The space industry has designed and built thruster systems, vent valves and even space station toilets for decades, so why are they still as unreliable as a 1970’s jalopy?

Media view

Despite all this, the Artemis II mission was probably good for STEM and has hopefully encouraged a large tranche of young people to engage with science, technology, engineering and maths. But the general media can’t take much credit for this. Much of the televised coverage in the UK (I can’t speak for coverage elsewhere) focused on the human aspects of the mission and any science done on the mission was mostly eclipsed.

While I fully appreciate that thrust coefficients and telemetry schedules have no place in public outreach, there is a tried-and-tested way to introduce lay audiences to the challenge and excitement of conducting a mission in an alien environment. In the UK, for Apollo, we were lucky to benefit from the guidance of the BBC’s James Burke, a journalist with no background in space technology but endowed with a professional ethic that demanded attention to detail. It’s clear from the BBC’s Artemis coverage that today’s ‘science correspondents’ lack this ability, or calling, to educate their audience - though, admittedly, they were not helped by NASA’s own public relations output, which concentrated on the human aspects of the mission.

A lack of technical appreciation was evident from the very beginning – the coverage of the launch. What I presume was NASA’s official feed, carried live by the TV networks, included moments of complete blackout following ignition and somehow managed to omit key moments, such as the vehicle clearing the tower and jettisoning its solid boosters; instead of the latter, an apparently bored producer showed us views of the crowd. One would think that these launch-sequence events were unpredictable, rather than timed to the second. Again, NASA’s public presentation of launches no longer feels as assured as it once did, while SpaceX in stark contrast, has it pretty much nailed.

Anyone who has ever followed a human space mission knows that the media’s focus on the Orion toilet was a given

Moreover, the NASA-organised ‘welcome home’ event at Houston was a pretty dire affair with its set speeches, read from autocue, overflowing with superlatives and devoid of humanity… that is, until the astronauts finally came on stage. It was only then that the event became bearable, touching, even thought-provoking at times.

Astronauts are famously professional and self-assured, even laid-back and laconic; they are the sort of people you would want with you in a disaster situation. But, watching the event, I felt that this crew had something more; possibly it was the media training they undoubtedly received, but also a personal confidence that allows one to be oneself whatever the pressures to perform.

Mission commander Reid Wiseman, for example, was not afraid to point out the obvious. Everyone in that room and watching remotely knew that these four people had just returned from a mission around the Moon – well, we’d all seen the figure-of-eight graphic a hundred times, hadn’t we? But when Wiseman pointed out, matter-of-factly, that since they’d boarded Orion 10 days earlier they had seen the Earth shrink as they powered towards the Moon, disappear as they orbited behind it and, later, grow larger in the window as they prepared for their fiery re-entry, I was suddenly there beside him.

However much one understands the mission trajectory intellectually, the realisation that the man on the stage was, just a few days earlier, a quarter of a million miles out in space, able to hide the rest of us behind his thumb was arresting, if not shocking.

Later in the show, Christina Koch’s thoughtful definition of a ‘crew’ was a valiant attempt to compare the four Artemis astronauts with the crew of ‘spaceship Earth’, hopeful perhaps that some leading politicians were listening and taking note. It’s often said that sending such politicians into orbit would convince them of the Earth’s fragility, even humanise them sufficiently to reduce global tensions, but perhaps that’s a hope for the future. It’s hard enough getting four career astronauts into orbit under the current regime!

The astronauts of the 1960s were characterised as having ‘the right stuff’ and today’s astronauts have that too, but they also have a different kind of stuff. In common with the modern-day man, male spacefarers are more in touch with their emotions and, thankfully, female astronauts are considered equals, which places 21st century astronauts ahead of their forerunners.

All that said, based on the outreach, I’m left with a feeling of ambivalence about their nine-day excursion. We were informed that the crew bonded well, enhanced their personal friendships and really enjoyed their time together in space, but is that commensurate with the price tag? Space proselytisers have enough trouble convincing naysayers as it is and I don’t believe that Artemis II helped our cause; the mission had the flavour of something between a modern-day reimagining and a makeover.

Politics and money

Clearly, any plans to send astronauts to the surface of the Moon (and later to Mars) will require more, not less, money

Now that the dust has settled on the Artemis II mission, it is time to look forward. Once again, however, I find myself questioning whether the Artemis programme will follow in the footsteps of Apollo, or suffer the same fate as the other failed NASA programmes to get ‘boots on the regolith’.

As usual, it’s all down to politics and money, in particular the current US Administration’s apparent intention to decimate the nation’s research and development efforts across a range of fields. As highlighted by Nature and other highly regarded journals, the plan proposes “cuts to federal agencies that fund or conduct research on health, space and the environment”. For example, the budgets of both the National Science Foundation and the Environmental Protection Agency would suffer reductions of “more than 50 percent” compared with current levels, while that for the National Institutes of Health would decrease by 13 percent.

But it’s the proposal to slash NASA’s budget by a quarter that concerns me here, as it provides limited confidence that later Artemis missions will actually place astronauts on the Moon (let alone on Mars, which is an order of magnitude more difficult). Nor am I encouraged by the NASA Administrator’s apparent acceptance of this cost-cutting stance. Publicly, at least, the agency’s leadership has appeared willing to work within the proposed budgetary constraints.

Clearly, any plans to send astronauts to the surface of the Moon (and later to Mars) will require more, not less, money. Surely, the conclusion of a successful and publicly well-received Artemis II mission is the time to call for a budget increase, or at least stability. Unfortunately, stability is not one of NASA’s core competencies. Following years of hype, the Lunar Gateway station was cancelled in March 2026, allegedly in favour of a permanent surface base. No doubt some of the bean-counters think that money saved on Gateway will fund Artemis, but this is just another example (after decades of cancelled technology developments) of the agency’s lack of resolve and staying power.

Even us armchair space explorers know that space exploration is not really about missions; it’s about providing the infrastructure for missions. While I had no particular feelings for the Gateway programme, the technology of its modules could have provided a stepping stone to the lunar surface and might also have been adapted for those future Mars missions.

Historians often point out that Russia has continually adapted its Soyuz spacecraft, learning and updating as it went, rather than developing entirely new vehicles. Many will remember that, when NASA retired the Space Shuttle fleet, it left itself with no homegrown spacecraft to ferry its astronauts to the International Space Station. Luckily, Soyuz had become part of the infrastructure and stepped into the breach, albeit at a predictably high cost-per-seat.

So why does NASA continually design from scratch and then ditch the technology and the institutional memory embodied in its educated workforce? The phrase “insanity is doing the same thing over and over again and expecting different results” is attributed to Einstein, apparently incorrectly, but it seems apt.

Elastic schedules

The closest parallel with those halcyon days of Apollo is the fear that another nation will get there first

My confidence in America’s ability to return people to the Moon is further diminished by the apparent lack of urgency. The Artemis III mission was to have placed astronauts on the surface, but that goal has slipped to Artemis IV. Instead, Artemis III will show that Orion can dock with one or more lunar landers in Earth orbit, in 2027, followed hopefully by a lunar landing in 2028.

A more charitable commentator might suggest that this was a sensible and safety-conscious correction to an aggressive schedule, but why was this docking phase not built into the programme as it was with Apollo? Probably because the commercially provided landers were ‘over-sold on schedule’ to NASA and are nowhere near ready, obliging the agency to insert a mission into the timeline to at least give the impression of progress.

But a mission a year is hardly aggressive and will do little to encourage either funding continuity or public acceptance. Apart from this, as is widely accepted in the industry, longer timelines mean higher overall mission costs - mostly because the largest cost in a space programme is the salary bill, and folks need paying even if the milestones slip to the right.

Channelling Apollo

Overall, it seems that we are not necessarily in a better place than we were in the Apollo days, even taking into account the delays imparted by the tragic Apollo 1 fire and the Apollo 13 explosion. In the 1960s, thanks to Kennedy’s end-of-the-decade deadline, NASA rose to the challenge and got the job done; clearly we live in a different world.

For one thing, we don’t have the level of visibility on progress, or lack of, that we had for Apollo. NASA contractors have become used to working in ‘stealth mode’, allowed to hide behind a veil of ‘commercial confidentiality’, apparently afraid to admit that space is hard. And, as implied above, media reporters simply haven’t the knowledge or experience to ask the right questions and investigate why SpaceX and Blue Origin aren’t being more transparent about delays to their lunar landers.

The closest parallel with those halcyon days of Apollo is the fear that another nation will get there first, but US politicians awoke far too late to the possibility that China could land a man or woman on the Moon before Artemis. Their extended nap means that it may already be too late for a sprint to the finish line.

Moreover, the promised one-mission-per-annum of the Artemis programme is not enough to make us, in Elon Musk’s words, a spacefaring civilisation. Whether or not it’s enough to beat China to the Moon, there is no guarantee that Artemis will continue beyond the first landing mission. Of course, we’ve been here before with the final three missions of the Apollo programme that were cancelled for political and financial reasons.

Apart from being twins in Greek mythology, Artemis and Apollo have many common elements, but I hope that a legacy of 50-plus years confined to low Earth orbit is not among them.

Artemis II demonstrated that NASA can once again send astronauts beyond low Earth orbit. That achievement deserves recognition. Whether Artemis ultimately becomes a sustained programme of exploration, however, will depend less on engineering than on political resolve, stable funding and a willingness to learn from the successes – and failures – of the past.

About the author

Mark Williamson is an independent Space Technology Consultant and writer, and a Commissioning Editor for ROOM Space Journal. He has 40 years of experience as a satellite communications engineer and consultant to the space industry, space insurance and space education sectors. He is the author of six books, including The Cambridge Dictionary of Space Technology and Space: The Fragile Frontier, has edited three space industry magazines and written more than 600 articles and papers on space technology. He has a BSc in physics and astrophysics, a PhD in sustainable development of the space environment and is a chartered physicist and chartered engineer. In 2008, Mark developed a sub-career as a stock photographer and currently licenses images across several platforms including Getty Images and Science Photo Library.

item.title: Artemis II rocket disrupted GPS signals, study finds - BBC
item.description:
While rocket launches usually tend to cause a bit of disruption to these types of signals, scientists say Artemis II's was more intense

  • Published

In April 2026, the world watched on as Artemis II took to the skies to study the Moon.

But a new study says the rocket launch disrupted part of the Earth's atmosphere and interrupted GPS signals that we use down on the ground.

GPS signals are made using satellites, and they help us do all kinds of things, like see where we are on maps on our phones.

GPS satellites can look like this - they also help us track and predict weather

A team of researchers from National Cheng Kung University in Taiwan looked at a GPS receivers on the ground in the US, and found that the power of the rocket's launch cause disturbances there more significant than any other rocket to date.

For example, the disruption to these signals was ten times more severe than the test launches of SpaceX's Starship.

More on Artemis II

What is Artemis?

Nina explains what the Artemis programme is all about

Artemis is NASA's newest Moon mission. They want to get astronauts back there for the first time since 1972.

It's happening in stages.

Artemis I took place in November 2022, and was used as a way to test all their kit, without anyone on board.

Artemis II, the one this new study refers to, saw a crew of four travel around the Moon in April 2026.

The crew on board Orion, the rocket used in Artemis II, sent back loads of photos of the Earth from Space like this one

Artemis III will be a bit closer to home, as a crew will fly into the upper prt of the Earth's atmosphere and practise some manoeuvres they'll need for the big finale.

And that is, of course, Artemis IIII, which will hopefully see a crew touch down on the Moon.

What are GPS signals?

Lots of navigation apps rely on GPS signals

GPS stands for Global Positioning System.

GPS satellites send out signals to say where they are above the Earth, which are then picked up by phones and other devices.

Whatever's being used to pick these signals up will figure out how long it took for the signal to reach them, and this timing shows how far away from each satellite the device is.

Your device needs to pick up at least four satellites to work out your exact location.

What happened with Artemis II?

Did you watch the Artemis II crew blast off?

The rocket disturbed a part of the Earth's atmosphere called the ionosphere, which is electrically charged.

When this layer is disrupted, by things like rockets or solar storms, it can make GPS signals get down to Earth far more slowly than they usually would.

And according to the authors of this new study published in Geophysical Research Letters, this happened intensely in two places above America with Artemis II.

Scientists say these disturbances could become more frequent in future

Charles Lin, an earth science professor at National Cheng Kung University and one of the co-authors of the paper, told science website Space.com these disruptions could have big effects on things that rely on GPS signals.

He said: "A positioning error of a couple of meters is enough to cause an autonomous car to change lanes.

"It could have a strong impact not only on self-driving cars but also on drone positioning."

He continued: "In the future, as we are going to see many more missions going to the moon and to Mars, these space weather effects will become much more significant."

item.title: Dream of a lifetime - Witnessing Artemis II from the Kennedy Space Center press site - Room The Space Journal of Asgardia
item.description:
Veteran space journalist Ken Kremer has spent decades reporting from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center. Earlier this year the Artemis II mission gave him the opportunity to witness something he had dreamed about since childhood – astronauts once again departing for the Moon. This is his personal reflection on a remarkable day in space history.

Some dreams stay with you for a lifetime. On 1 April 2026, standing beside the current iteration of NASA’s famous Countdown Clock at the Kennedy Space Center Press Site, one of mine finally came true. As Artemis II thundered into the Florida sky carrying four astronauts on humanity’s first crewed journey towards the Moon in more than half a century, I realised I was witnessing history.

This time I wasn’t watching on a television screen. I was there as a journalist – photographing, reporting and sharing one of the most significant milestones in human spaceflight since Apollo.

For me, Artemis II was much more than another launch. It was the culmination of a lifelong fascination with space exploration that began as a young boy growing up in New York during the Apollo era.

Like millions around the world, I was captivated by President Kennedy’s vision, NASA’s achievements and the extraordinary courage of the astronauts who ventured into the unknown. I watched every Mercury, Gemini, Apollo and Skylab mission, read everything I could find about space exploration and vividly remember gazing up at the Moon during the Apollo missions, imagining the explorers making history hundreds of thousands of miles away.

Those early years shaped my outlook on science, exploration and discovery. They also inspired dreams of becoming an astronaut myself. Reality, of course, had other ideas.

As the Apollo programme came to an end and NASA’s ambitions were scaled back, I turned my passion for science into a career, becoming a research chemist working in the United States, Germany, France, Switzerland, Italy and Argentina. Although my professional life took a different direction, my fascination with space never diminished and eventually it found another outlet.

For me Artemis II was much more than another launch. It was the culmination of a lifelong fascination with space exploration that began as a young boy growing up in New York

Some two decades ago I began covering launches and planetary missions from the Kennedy Space Center, combining my scientific background with journalism and photography. What started as an opportunity soon became a second career.

The Space Shuttle era gave me a front row seat to some of NASA’s most remarkable achievements and I was privileged to report on numerous Shuttle launches and landings, witnessing first-hand the extraordinary complexity of human spaceflight and the dedication of the thousands of people who made every mission possible. It also opened doors to spacecraft processing facilities, astronaut interviews and mission briefings, providing an insider’s view of America’s space programme that I could only once have dreamed about.

Those years covering the Shuttle programme shaped my approach as a space journalist. They also reinforced an uncomfortable reality. Following the Shuttle’s retirement in 2011, the United States – at least until the human-rated SpaceX Falcon 9 came along – no longer had the capability to launch its own astronauts into deep space. The Moon once again seemed frustratingly distant.

Artemis changed that and the programme represents something unique. For the first time since Apollo 17 left the Moon in December 1972, astronauts are once again venturing beyond low Earth orbit (LEO). Artemis II was a crucial step to demonstrate the Orion spacecraft and Space Launch System could safely carry people around the Moon and back to Earth. It marked the beginning of humanity’s return to deep space.

Having followed the programme through years of development, delays, engineering challenges and countless media briefings, finally seeing the completed vehicle standing on Launch Complex 39B ready for liftoff was a deeply emotional experience.

In the days leading up to countdown I had the opportunity to meet the four Artemis II astronauts on several occasions, listen to their thoughts about the mission and ask questions during media events. Their enthusiasm was infectious and their sense of responsibility unmistakable. Together they represented not only the USA and Canada, but an entirely new generation of explorers.

Launch day itself exceeded every expectation. Watching the 98-metre-tall Space Launch System (SLS) ignite in broad daylight is an experience almost impossible to describe. The brilliant flash from the engines momentarily overwhelmed both eyes and cameras before the deep rumble arrived, building into an ear-splitting roar that shook the ground beneath us.

Slowly at first, then gathering speed, the giant rocket climbed above the launch pad, arcing gracefully into the Florida sky on its journey towards the Moon.

I had cameras positioned around the launch complex as well as several with me at the Press Site but, for a few unforgettable moments, photography became secondary. Like everyone around me, I simply watched. After waiting more than 50 years to witness astronauts depart for the Moon, I wanted to absorb every second.

Artemis II also reminds us that exploration is a long game. More than 50 years separated Apollo 17 from humanity’s return to lunar space

The mission itself surpassed expectations. During their 10-day flight the crew travelled around the far side of the Moon, returning spectacular imagery and reminding the world just how inspiring human exploration can be. Their safe return represented the culmination of years of work by thousands of engineers, technicians, scientists and support staff whose dedication made the mission possible.

As a journalist, I have always believed that space exploration is about far more than rockets and spacecraft. It is about curiosity, international cooperation, scientific discovery and inspiring future generations to look beyond today’s challenges.

Throughout my career I have tried to help tell those stories, whether reporting from launch sites, visiting spacecraft processing facilities or explaining complex missions to audiences around the world. If even a handful of young people are encouraged to pursue careers in science or engineering because of that work, I consider it time well spent.

Artemis II also reminds us that exploration is a long game. More than 50 years separated Apollo 17 from humanity’s return to lunar space. Progress has not always been straightforward and there have been many setbacks along the way. But the desire to explore has endured.

Standing at Kennedy Space Center watching the SLS disappear into the brilliant blue Florida sky, I found myself thinking back to the young boy who had watched Apollo on television all those years ago.

He could never have imagined that one day he would stand beside NASA’s iconic Countdown Clock, camera in hand, reporting humanity’s return to the Moon. After more than half a century it was a dream that had finally come true.

About the author

Dr Ken Kremer is a pharmaceutical research chemist, space journalist, photographer and Founder/Managing Editor of Space UpClose. Based on Florida’s Space Coast near NASA’s Kennedy Space Center, he has covered human and robotic spaceflight for more than two decades and has witnessed over 400 rocket launches. He has written more than 1800 articles on space exploration, contributed 14 NASA Astronomy Picture of the Day (APOD) selections and regularly provides independent commentary on spaceflight for television and radio broadcasters, including ABC, BBC, CBS, NBC, PBS, Sky News and Fox News. He holds 15 US patents, has authored more than 30 scientific publications and was awarded NASA’s Curiosity medallion for his contributions to science outreach and Mars panorama imaging.

item.title: NASA Releases Artemis II Lunar Science Data, Images - NASA (.gov)
item.description:
NASA Releases Artemis II Lunar Science Data, Images

NASA’s Artemis II crew traveled around the Moon and back and, along the way, captured stunning imagery and scientific observations of our nearest neighbor. NASA is making the full lunar science dataset from their journey available Wednesday to the global science community and the public for further study.

More than 800 gigabytes of Artemis II lunar science data – some previously unreleased – have been uploaded to NASA’s Planetary Data System, the public archive for NASA’s planetary missions. This data release includes more than 11,000 full-resolution images and video of the Moon from the crew’s handheld cameras and the Orion spacecraft’s cameras, 8.5 hours of audio recordings of the crew’s scientific observations of the lunar surface, and crew-annotated images.

When combined, the images, audio files, and crew notes from the expedition provide a powerful lunar science dataset ripe for exploration and analysis. This is the first planetary science dataset captured primarily by humans in more than half a century and humanity’s influence on it is clear. Through training in classrooms, simulations, and field environments, NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, and Christina Koch, and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Jeremy Hansen developed expertise in lunar geography, geology, and observational best practices. Their quick decisions about observation targets and which images to capture, along with their perceptions of color and dynamic changes, and discussions about the science of the lunar surface and its surroundings complement decades of data from Apollo astronauts and robotic explorers and deepen our understanding of the Moon as NASA prepares for long-term exploration of the lunar surface.

Along with this data, NASA has released the Artemis II Preliminary Lunar Science Report, the Artemis II Lunar Science Operations Report, and the Artemis II Lunar Science Data User Guide. Together, these three publications provide an overview of the Artemis II lunar mission data and activities, and a technical summary of how the science plan was developed and implemented. This information is already helping inform NASA’s exploration plans for Artemis III and beyond.

item.title: NASA's Artemis II rocket punched 3,100-mile-long holes in Earth's atmosphere, disrupted GPS signals: Study - The Economic Times
item.description:
According to a report by Space.com, a team of researchers from Taiwan's National Cheng Kung University found that the atmospheric impact of the Artemis II launch was significantly more intense than that of earlier rocket launches. The researchers said the disturbances were up to 10 times more intense than those observed after SpaceX's Starship test launches, despite Starship having roughly twice the liftoff thrust of NASA's Space Launch System (SLS) rocket.

Artemis II launch disrupted GPS signals

Ground-based GPS stations detected changes in electron density in Earth's ionosphere during the launch. These disturbances were equivalent to positioning errors of several metres. Such inaccuracies could have serious implications for technologies that depend on precise location data, including self-driving cars and drones.

Charles Lin, an Earth science professor at National Cheng Kung University and one of the study's co-authors, warned that even a small positioning error could affect autonomous vehicles. "A positioning error of a couple of meters is enough to cause an autonomous car to change lanes," Lin told Space.com. He added that the disturbances could also affect drone positioning.

Researchers identified two large atmospheric disturbances following the launch. The first was associated with the rocket's 212-foot-long (65-metre) core stage, while the second followed two subsequent thruster burns by the upper stage. Both disturbances extended across the American continent from east to west, covering distances of approximately 3,100 miles (5,000 kilometres).

Why did Artemis II create holes in Earth's atmosphere?

The disturbances occurred in the ionosphere, an electrically charged region of Earth's upper atmosphere that plays an important role in radio communication and satellite-based navigation.

However, the scale of the disturbances associated with Artemis II has raised questions about how increasingly powerful rocket launches could affect satellite navigation and other technologies.

Artemis II: A historic mission to the Moon

NASA's Artemis II mission carried four astronauts — Christina Koch, Victor Glover, Jeremy Hansen and Reid Wiseman — on a journey around the Moon. The crew included the first woman, the first person of colour and the first non-American astronaut to participate in a crewed lunar mission.

The mission also set a new record for the greatest distance humans have travelled from Earth. The astronauts reached approximately 252,756 miles (406,771 kilometres), surpassing the record set by Apollo 13 in 1970 by more than 4,000 miles.

Another highlight was the crew's photographs of Earth from space, including an image dubbed 'Earthset', which showed the planet appearing to disappear behind the Moon.

The astronauts also witnessed a solar eclipse from space and reported flashes of light believed to be meteorite impacts on the lunar surface.

They flew around the Moon's far side at an altitude of approximately 4,000 miles, offering a different perspective of the lunar landscape from the one available to the Apollo astronauts.

### What comes next for NASA's Artemis programme?

Artemis II was the first crewed flight of NASA's Space Launch System rocket and Orion spacecraft. The mission was designed to test the systems and procedures needed for future human lunar exploration.

NASA's broader Artemis programme aims to return astronauts to the lunar surface and establish a sustained human presence on the Moon, potentially creating a foundation for future crewed missions to Mars.

The programme is also unfolding against renewed competition in space exploration, with China aiming to send astronauts to the Moon by 2030.

The findings on the Artemis II launch add another dimension to the challenges of increasingly powerful space missions. While rocket-induced atmospheric disturbances are temporary, their potential effects on GPS-dependent technologies could become an important consideration as launch activity increases.

item.title: 'Dude! No way!' Scientists jump for joy over Artemis II moon science results - Space
item.description:
We have our first look at the science from Artemis II, and it's as amazing as we might have hoped.

This past April, four astronauts strapped in for a flyby around the moon and back to Earth. The first mission to the moon since the Apollo program ended in 1972, this success marked an incredible historic milestone. The Artemis II crew also conducted groundbreaking science, observing parts of the moon no human had ever laid eyes on before. And now, we have our first look at some of the science from the mission.

"It's the science community's job now to take these data and go do magical things with it," David Hollibaugh Baker, a member of the Artemis II Lunar Science Team, said during a Wednesday (10/7) press conference that announced the mission's initial science results.

This is just the first batch of data from the mission, but it includes a whopping 996 new images, 814 GB of observations and 521 minutes of audio from the crew that has never been heard before. Everything from that astronauts' handwritten notes and drawings to photographs and verbal observations have revealed exciting new information — about impact flashes on the moon, for example, as well as the terminator line between the lunar "day" and "night" sides and a whole range of lunar colors and observations from beyond the mysterious far side.

Let's take a quick look at some of the highlights.

Impact flashes

"Dude, no way!" Artemis II commander Reid Wiseman of NASA exclaimed in newly released mission audio.

"It's just like a 'bloop!'" mission specialist Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency added as the flashes appeared on the lunar surface. .

As Artemis II's Orion capsule flew by the moon, the four astronauts onboard — Wiseman, Hansen and NASA astronauts Victor Glover (mission pilot) and Christina Koch (mission specialist)— started seeing flashes of light on the lunar surface. These were impact flashes caused by small rocks hitting the lunar surface and vaporizing in the impact.

"We have seen three impact flashes so far," Wiseman said to Mission Control at NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston. "It was not sun glint off a particulate from the thrusters or the purge tanks. It was definitely impact flashes on the moon."

"Amazing news," Mission Control responded. "I literally just looked over at the SER [Science Evaluation Room], and they were jumping up and down, literally."

In total, the crew saw five impact flashes on the moon's surface, which the mission's science team was able to confirm didn't come from other sources.

While the Artemis II crew was equipped with cameras, they were also trained to make observations with the unaided eye. And impact flashes happen too quickly to photograph them, so — as you can see above — the crew used a tablet to make annotations and describe their observations.

"We wanted them to look visually, so there are not camera images of that, but we have their annotations of when they saw them," Jennifer Heldmen, science theme lead for the Artemis II mission, said during the briefing.

A rainbow moon

In addition to seeing impact flashes across the lunar surface, the Artemis II crew observed a wide range of colors on the moon.

Looking up in the night sky, it might seem that the moon is just shades of gray. But as the astronauts saw during their flyby, the moon is gray, black, brown, tan, white, green and even blue. This muted rainbow of colors was not only visually striking, as the astronauts' photos show, but it can also help scientists determine what types of rocks and minerals might be found in different regions across the moon's surface.

"The crew reported greens and yellowish hues on top of Aristarchus Plateau, signaling they were seeing remnants of different styles and epochs of volcanic activity, and the crew contrasted those colors to nearby browns and grays of adjacent volcanic plains," Ariel Deutsch, a member of the Artemis II Lunar Science Team, said during the briefing, givingone example of these colorful observations.

"To me, it's primarily like a brownish-green glass, and then if I went up into the mares [dark volcanic deposits] to the north of Aristarchus, I would give that a very muted brown," Wiseman said in mission recordings shared in this release.

"It's like a jaundiced cheek of the moon," Koch remarked in mission audio, describing yellowish colors on the moon.

And while the crew took some amazing photographs of the moon, in this data release we can also see their handwritten notes annotating the colors they saw on the moon.

The far side of the moon

As the moon is tidally locked to Earth, it has one "day side" that always faces us and one far or "night side" that is always facing away. When the Artemis II astronauts flew by the moon, they flew around the entire object, even around the far side. During their flyby, they were able to see a part of the far sidethat has never been observed up close like this before.

"The Artemis II crew were the first people to see this section of the moon illuminated in all of human history," Alex Stoken, a member of the Crew Lunar Observations team, said during the briefing.

When they approached the moon's far side, the crew also came upon the terminator line, or the boundary between the day and night sides of the moon.

At the terminator, the team was able to view the incredible contrasting shadows and textures of the lunar surface, revealing sharp details about the moon's topography.

"The terminator is the most striking thing that I’ve seen so far," Glover said as the crew flew by.

As they rounded the moon's far side, the moon was backlit by the sun, essentially eclipsing it. This allowed for incredibly unique and sharp views of the moon.

"You’ve got to be kidding me," Koch said in the capsule. "You can actually see mountains."

These are just a few highlights from this incredibly thorough and detailed data release. As we dig deeper into this initial science, you can take a dive through the data yourself here and here.

Chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. When not writing, editing or filming something space-y, Gohd is writing music and performing as Foxanne, even launching a song to space in 2021 with Inspiration4. item.title: NASA’s Artemis II moon mission punched 5,000-km-wide holes in Earth’s atmosphere. Here’s why it matters - CNBC TV18
item.description:
NASA’s Artemis II moon mission punched 5,000-km-wide holes in Earth’s atmosphere. Here’s why it matters

Heavy-lift rocket launches are generating artificial space weather by creating massive disturbances in the upper atmosphere, altering signal travel times and threatening high-precision satellite navigation. Find out how researchers plan to monitor these human-made disruptions as launch frequencies accelerate.

When NASA’s Artemis II mission lifted off on its historic crewed lunar flyby, it did more than break distance records. It also created temporary disturbances stretching 3,100 miles (5,000 kilometres) across Earth's upper atmosphere.

According to a recent study by researchers at Taiwan's National Cheng Kung University, the powerful core-stage ascent and subsequent upper-stage engine burns created intense atmospheric disturbances inside the ionosphere, the electrically charged layer of the upper atmosphere.

The ionosphere begins roughly 50 kilometres above Earth's surface and extends hundreds of kilometres into space. It plays an important role in radio communications and satellite navigation because charged particles in this layer can influence the signals travelling between satellites and receivers on the ground.

Crucially, the study found that these artificial disturbances were significantly more powerful than those recorded following previous heavy-lift rocket launches. Researchers identified three separate disturbances associated with the mission's launch and subsequent engine burns, making it an unusual case of repeated atmospheric disruption over the same geographical region.

The resulting thinning of charged particles altered the time taken for satellite signals to travel through the atmosphere, potentially introducing metre-scale GPS positioning errors across North America.

This happens because GPS receivers calculate their location by measuring how long signals take to travel from orbiting satellites to the ground. Changes in the ionosphere's electron density can alter signal travel times, causing receivers to miscalculate distances and, consequently, their positions.

While consumer mapping apps and turn-by-turn driving directions can accommodate minor positioning fluctuations, high-precision applications such as autonomous vehicle navigation, drone operations and precision surveying could face reliability risks when space weather and rocket-induced disruptions occur together.

The researchers, however, have not established that the Artemis II launch caused widespread GPS failures or accidents. The positioning errors are potential consequences inferred from the atmospheric disturbances observed in the study.

As lunar and interplanetary launches become more frequent, scientists say monitoring and managing these human-made disturbances in the ionosphere will become increasingly important to safeguarding ground-based and orbital navigation systems.

The findings also highlight a relatively overlooked consequence of the growing space industry: rockets can generate their own form of 'space weather', potentially affecting technologies that depend on uninterrupted satellite signals.

item.title: Artemis II Crew Moon Photo Annotations - NASA (.gov)
item.description:
A visualization of a dark Moon eclipsing the Sun is marked with handwritten notes in this April 6, 2026, screenshot from an Artemis II crew member’s tablet.

NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman (in blue) and Victor “Ike” Glover (in green) and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) Jeremy Hansen (in red) observed impact flashes and their locations, which are noted on the image. Overall, the astronauts reported seeing five extremely faint “pinprick” bursts of light from their view aboard Orion, which was 46,000 miles away from the Moon at the time. These flashes are sparked by rocky fragments hitting the Moon.

From April 1 through April 10, 2026, NASA’s Artemis II crew traveled to the Moon and back and along the way, captured stunning imagery and scientific observations of our nearest neighbor. Now, the full lunar science dataset from their journey is available to the global science community, and to the public, for further study. Read about the report, listen to crew audio observations, and explore more.

item.title: NASA Names Two Artemis II Astronauts to Emeritus Program - NASA (.gov)
item.description:
Following their landmark Artemis II mission earlier this year, distinguished NASA astronauts Victor Glover and Reid Wiseman are transitioning in September to emeritus status at the agency’s Johnson Space Center in Houston.

In an emeritus role, individuals with a high degree of technical and professional knowledge can continue to support the agency by donating their time to train and mentor the current workforce. This allows the agency to maintain access to top talent in a specialized consultant role, while simultaneously providing the individual with the flexibility to pursue other opportunities.

“I’ve had the privilege of knowing Reid and Victor for years, and both exemplify the leadership, character, and commitment that define NASA at its best.” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “Reid commanded Artemis II after previously spending 165 days aboard the International Space Station, while Victor brought his experience as a naval aviator, test pilot, and Crew-1 astronaut to his role as pilot. Together, they took on one of the most challenging missions in human spaceflight and helped return America to the lunar environment. As Reid and Victor transition to emeritus status, I’m grateful they will continue sharing what they learned with our astronauts, flight controllers, and engineers as we prepare for Artemis III in 2027 and the missions that follow.”

Glover will support aerospace, leadership, and public service efforts as he transitions within and outside of NASA. He’s committed to transferring his knowledge of Orion and its spacecraft systems, among other expertise, to future Artemis missions.

“As I grow into this new role, NASA and spaceflight remain a meaningful part of my journey of service,” said Glover. “I’m excited to keep uplifting my friends and cheering them on as they reach for the Moon. Together, we’ll keep pushing boundaries and inspiring the next giant leap.”

Wiseman is set to share his spaceflight experience with colleagues ahead of the agency’s Artemis III mission in low Earth orbit to test rendezvous and docking capabilities between Orion and commercial human landing systems.

“There is no better place to work, and there are no better people to work with, than those in this agency,” said Wiseman. “NASA gave me tremendous responsibility, supported me through two space missions, and my time as chief astronaut, and was always there for my family when we needed it most. I’m thrilled to continue serving future missions and programs through the emeritus program.”

“Reid and Victor’s commitment to exploration, steady leadership, and service to our astronaut corps and our nation have made a lasting impact,” said Vanessa Wyche, director of NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. “Throughout their careers, they have each brought excellence, humility, and purpose to every role they have held at NASA. Their contributions have helped advance our mission and inspire those around them, leaving a legacy that will continue to shape the future of human spaceflight. We are immeasurably grateful for all they have given to NASA and are glad that this is not the end of their journey with the agency.”

“Reid and Victor are trusted teammates whose professionalism, calm leadership, and unwavering commitment to NASA have strengthened our office and inspired everyone around them,” said Scott Tingle, chief of the Astronaut Office at Johnson. “As they transition into their emeritus roles, they leave a legacy of operational excellence that will continue shaping the astronaut corps for years to come. We’re grateful that they will still be part of our community, sharing their experience and insight as they begin this next chapter.”

Among their many accomplishments at NASA, as Artemis II crew members, Glover and Wiseman were two of the four astronauts to first launch on top NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket aboard the Orion spacecraft for a mission around the Moon. Following a 10-day mission with crewmates NASA astronaut Christina Koch and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Jeremy Hansen, they safely splashed down on April 10 as the first humans to travel to lunar orbit in more than 50 years, ultimately flying farther in space than anyone had before.

Support and knowledge transfer from both Glover and Wiseman is critical for the upcoming Artemis III mission as NASA prepares to return American astronauts to the lunar surface on the Artemis IV mission in 2028.
